title: Record of a Boat Trip to Wu
subtitle: Fan Chengda · Eastward Down the Yangtze from Chengdu · A Myriad-Mile Homeward Journey
description: Fan Chengda (1126–1193), courtesy name Zhineng, sobriquet Shihu Jushi, was born in Wu County, Pingjiang Prefecture (present-day Suzhou, Jiangsu), one of the Four Great Poets of the Southern Song's中兴. In the fourth year of the Chunxi reign (1177), the fifty-two-year-old Fan Chengda departed from his post in Chengdu and traveled eastward home along the Min and Yangtze Rivers, arriving in Lin'an after several months. He recorded his journey in the two-volume Record of a Boat Trip to Wu, capturing the landscapes, ancient sites, and local customs along the way. This route follows Fan Chengda's homeward boat journey, visiting the nationally protected heritage sites that witnessed the poet's downstream verse.

route.title: Record of a Boat Trip to Wu: Fan Chengda's Ten-Thousand-Mile Voyage Home, from the Land of Abundance to the Watery South
route.intro:
The perils of the Shu River—I have experienced them myself. Yet sailing through it was like traversing level ground.
In the first year of the Chunxi reign (1174), Fan Chengda was appointed Military Commissioner of Sichuan—equivalent to the commander-in-chief and governor of the region. He served for three years in Chengdu, building irrigation works, reducing taxes, and earning the gratitude of the Shu people. In the fourth year of Chunxi (1177), the court summoned him back to Lin'an (Hangzhou). He bade farewell to his colleagues and the people of Chengdu, hired a large boat, loaded it with books and simple luggage, and sailed down the Min River—completing this "ten-thousand-mile homeward journey." Fan Chengda was a poet "on the road." He had served as an envoy to the Jin kingdom, writing Record of Grasping the Reins; governed in Guilin, writing Records of the Seas and Mountains of Gui; and after retirement lived by Stone Lake, writing Records of Wu Commanderies. But Record of a Boat Trip to Wu is his most personal and relaxed travelogue—the journey here was anxious, the journey home was calm, and everything he wrote bore the warm hues of homecoming. Let us board the boat and sail with Fan Chengda, from Chengdu back to Jiangnan, amid the sounds of the river and the light of the moon.

stops.title: Stop One: Chengdu—Where Is the Prime Minister's Shrine?
stops.content: Before departing his post, Fan Chengda made a point of visiting the two most sacred sites in Chengdu. He first went to the Chengdu Wuhou Shrine, the combined temple commemorating Zhuge Liang and Liu Bei. As a high-ranking military and civil official, Fan Chengda held deep respect for Zhuge Liang's "dedication to the utmost, unto death." He wandered leisurely in the shrine, gazing at the gray-green cypress trees on Huiling, perhaps recalling Du Fu's lines: "Where is the Prime Minister's shrine to be found? Outside Jinguan City, among cypress trees deep and profound." Leaving Wuhou Shrine, he went to the Chengdu Du Fu Thatched Cottage by the banks of Huanhua Stream. Though Fan Chengda lived more than four hundred years after Du Fu, they were both poets who sojourned in Shu, and their shared sentiment of "how can I get a vast mansion for all the world's poor" resonated across the centuries. The thatched cottage's bamboo groves, little bridges, and flowing waters reminded him of his own Stone Lake home in Suzhou—home was now within reach. On the day he boarded his boat, his Chengdu friends held a farewell feast at Hejiang Pavilion. After several rounds of wine, Fan Chengda dashed off "The road to Shu is harder than the road to Heaven"—this time he was traveling by water, but his poetic sentiment was just as intense. In his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu, Fan Chengda's depiction of Chengdu carries a profound sense of parting. He recorded Chengdu's "Twelve Monthly Fairs"—the Lantern Fair in the first month, the Flower Fair in the second, the Silkworm Fair in the third—a different theme every month, bringing the vitality of the millennia-old Brocade City vividly to life. At Wuhou Shrine, he paid special attention to the Tang stele—the "Three Perfections Stele" composed by Pei Du, written by Liu Gongchuo, and carved by Lu Jian: "Its prose is elegant, its characters vigorous—the finest stele in all of Shu." Leaving Wuhou Shrine, he strolled along the Jin River to Hejiang Pavilion—at the confluence of two rivers, white egrets wheeled, and the distant western mountains still bore unmelted snow. "Though Brocade City offers pleasures, home is best," as Li Bai's verse put it—perfectly capturing his mood. During his three years as Military Commissioner of Sichuan, Chengda not only repaired the irrigation works at the Dujiangyan, but also left many public works projects in the city. The Record of a Boat Trip to Wu opens with the words: "Shihu Jushi departed Chengdu on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month of the dingyou year of the Chunxi reign"—just a few words, but his gratitude for the three years in Shu is implicit.

stops.title: Stop Two: Meishan—Remembering Dongpo at the Three Sus Shrine
stops.content: The boat sailed south along the Min River and soon reached Meishan—the hometown of Su Xun, Su Shi, and Su Zhe. Fan Chengda was an ardent fan of Su Shi; how could he pass through Meishan without going ashore to pay homage? The Three Sus Shrine stood in the heart of Meishan, originally the Su family home, later converted into a shrine. "A myriad bamboos before the gate, the books of the Three Sus in the hall"—the garden was full of ancient trees, surrounded by bamboo groves, and a pond reflecting the image of young Dongpo at his studies. Fan Chengda wrote in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu: "The former residence of the Su family in Meishan has a shrine, which still stands"—just a few words, but the respect is unmistakable. Fan Chengda must have thought of Su Shi's life—setting out from Meishan for the wider world, exiled three times, each time farther than the last, yet never bowing his head. "A straw cloak, a misty rain, I travel through life at ease"—Fan Chengda himself had endured no small amount of official hardship. Now, sailing eastward with the current, he felt a touch of Dongpo's carefree spirit. In Fan Chengda's time, the Three Sus Shrine was still modest in scale, just a family shrine, "though its gate and courtyard are narrow, the bamboo and trees are lush." But Fan Chengda's description of Meishan in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu is remarkably warm: "Meishan, ancient Meizhou, has the Su family's former residence." He noted the "ancient well" before the shrine—legend had it that Su Xun drew water from this well to teach his sons to read and write: "The spring is sweet and cool, perfect for tea." Fan Chengda ordered his attendant to draw a bucket of well water to brew tea. Amid the fragrant steam, he seemed to see the young Su Shi and Su Zhe at their studies. Today, the Three Sus Shrine has been expanded into a classical garden covering more than sixty thousand square meters—with "three parts water, two parts bamboo," a living embodiment of Dongpo's line "Better to eat without meat than to live without bamboo." The shrine houses thousands of calligraphic works and documents by the three Sus, among which the rubbing of Su Shi's "Cold Food Observance" is world-famous—"The palace gate is nine layers deep; my ancestors' graves lie ten thousand miles away"—the page is steeped in sorrow yet exudes an indomitable spirit. The well-water tea that Fan Chengda drank before the Three Sus Shrine was more than tea—it was the very character of three generations of the Su family.

stops.title: Stop Three: Leshan—Where Three Rivers Converge at the Great Buddha's Feet
stops.content: The boat reached Jiazhou (present-day Leshan), and Fan Chengda's gaze was drawn to a colossal Buddha carved into the cliff of Lingyun Mountain—the Leshan Giant Buddha, seventy-one meters tall, the world's largest cliff-carved seated Maitreya Buddha. His Record of a Boat Trip to Wu records in detail his impression of the Great Buddha: "The Buddha image is several tens of zhang tall, from head to toe carved entirely from the mountain." He was utterly awestruck by its scale. At the Buddha's feet, the Min, Qingyi, and Dadu Rivers converge in surging waves. It was precisely because of the countless ships capsized by the three rivers that the Tang monk Haitong had made the vow to "carve the Buddha into the mountain to calm the waters," even gouging out his own eyes to demonstrate his resolve. Fan Chengda pressed his palms together before the Great Buddha and silently prayed for a smooth voyage. He was not a Buddhist, but he understood this kind of determined persistence—the same feeling he had when building irrigation works and benefiting the people in Sichuan. The Great Buddha's compassionate gaze saw his boat off into the Yangtze. Fan Chengda's record of the Leshan Giant Buddha in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu is so detailed that it has become a primary source for later studies of the Great Buddha. He noted not only its height, but also that "several people can sit or lie down inside the Buddha's ear"—one of the Buddha's ears was as large as a room. He wrote specially about the story of the Buddha's builder: when Monk Haitong gouged out his own eyes to raise funds for the statue, "those who saw it could not hold back their tears." Construction began in the first year of the Kaiyuan reign (713) and was completed in the nineteenth year of the Zhenyuan reign (803), spanning ninety years—three generations, one after another, until the world's largest stone-carved Buddha stood proud at the confluence of three rivers. Embedded in the Leshan Giant Buddha's torso is an ingenious drainage system—hidden channels in the Buddha's coiled hair, behind its ears, and within its collar rapidly channel rainwater away, protecting the carving from erosion. Fan Chengda naturally did not discover this secret, but he marveled in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu: "Though the Buddha image is colossal, its eyes and brows convey a spirit of compassion." This was precisely Monk Haitong's original intention: to calm the waters with the Great Buddha, and to save all beings with great compassion. From Fan Chengda's boat to the tour ships of today, every traveler passing Leshan slows down at the Great Buddha's feet—in that moment of looking up, one forgets one's own insignificance and feels only a gentle shelter.

stops.title: Stop Four: Chongqing—Mountain City Nightscape and Ba-Yu Charm
stops.content: The boat entered Gongzhou (present-day Chongqing), a mountain city at the confluence of the Yangtze and Jialing Rivers. Fan Chengda's description of Chongqing in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu is extraordinarily vivid—layer upon layer of stilted houses clinging to the mountainside, a ceaseless flow of people on the docks, boat trackers' chants shaking the heavens. "A myriad lamps cast a red glow upon the river"—his depiction of Chongqing's night scene remains vivid more than eight hundred years later. Chongqing was then a major military stronghold in eastern Sichuan, with formidable defenses. Fan Chengda, as former Military Commissioner of Sichuan, inspected the city's fortifications. He saw the cliff walls along the river densely covered with inscriptions from successive dynasties—some praising the landscape, others recording military achievements. The Ba-Yu region had been a land of heroes since ancient times, from Ba Manzi to Zhang Fei; the spirit of loyalty and righteousness echoed in the river breeze. After a brief stop in Chongqing, the boat continued eastward. This stretch was the most perilous of the Three Gorges—Fan Chengda stood at the prow, facing into the wind, green mountains on both banks receding like galloping horses, the river thundering like rolling drums. In the Song dynasty, Chongqing was called Gongzhou, the fiefdom of Emperor Guangzong of Song before his enthronement. Upon ascending the throne, he renamed Gongzhou to Chongqing Prefecture, meaning "double celebration"—and the name Chongqing was born. Fan Chengda did not write extensively about Chongqing in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu, but his brushstrokes are exceptionally vivid: "The mountain city is built against the cliffs, houses piled like stacked eggs"—the spectacle of stilted buildings amazed this man from the watery south. He also noted the city's seventeen gates, "nine open, eight closed"—each gate corresponding to a dock, "a thousand boats swarming daily like ants." Upstream from Chongqing, on Fishing Mountain in Hechuan District, stands the Diaoyu Fortress Site, which changed the course of world history. This Southern Song fortress that resisted Mongol invasion became "the place where God broke His whip"—in 1259, the Mongol Great Khan Mongke died here, rewriting the geopolitical map of Eurasia. Fan Chengda did not climb Fishing Mountain, but he noted in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu the river defense situation at Hezhou (present-day Hechuan): "On both banks are mountains; the river narrows to a single passage—a strategically perilous terrain." This was the geographic secret of Diaoyu Fortress's thirty-six-year defense. From Chongqing's city gates to Diaoyu's ramparts, the spirit of Ba-Yu loyalty flickers subtly in Fan Chengda's writing, just as he wrote in his poems: "A myriad miles of river, swift as an arrow; a thousand years of rise and fall, a single sigh."

stops.title: Stop Five: Yichang—Meeting the Three Wandering Immortals Cave Again
stops.content: Emerging from the Three Gorges, the river opened up into a broad expanse. At the mouth of Xiling Gorge, at the Three Wandering Immortals Cave Cliff Inscriptions, Fan Chengda, like Lu You before him, crept into the cave to admire the inscriptions of his predecessors. He and Lu You were close friends—two of the "Four Great Poets of the Southern Song Restoration"—and he searched specifically for the ink traces that Lu You had left seven years earlier. His Record of a Boat Trip to Wu reads: "In the cave are the inscriptions of the Three Sus, the characters still intact." When Fan Chengda saw the names of Su Xun, Su Shi, and Su Zhe, he was more moved than by any scenic view. He was a poet, and to him, words on stone were more precious than the stone itself. He lingered in the cave for a long time, perhaps even reciting a few verses—but the Record of a Boat Trip to Wu records only prose. Leaving the Three Wandering Immortals Cave, ahead lay the flat, open plain of Jianghan. The most perilous part of the Three Gorges was behind him, and Fan Chengda's heart was completely at ease. His boat glided smoothly on the broad river, with peach blossoms in full bloom on both banks. The cave is not large, but the abundance of its stone inscriptions is astonishing. Fan Chengda wrote in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu: "The stone walls of the cave are covered with poems and prose from former worthies, leaving scarcely an empty space"—a testament to how densely packed the cliff inscriptions had already become in the Southern Song. He recorded in particular Bai Juyi's inscription: "Bai Letian, together with his younger brother Zhitui and Yuan Weizhi, gathered at Yiling"—this is the original record of the "former three wanderers." The Three Sus' inscription had Su Xun in the center, Su Shi on the left, and Su Zhe on the right, "the characters reflecting the men, each with his own style." Fan Chengda stood long beside Su Shi's inscription, perhaps murmuring to himself: "Master Dongpo, though I was born decades after you, I have admired your character all my life." The Sanyou Dong cliff inscription group is now a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level—more than two hundred inscriptions from the Tang and Song dynasties to the Republic of China, layer upon layer, forming the most important gallery of calligraphic art in the Three Gorges. The cave contains not only poems and literary inscriptions, but also war records, hydrological markers, and road-building inscriptions—within a small space, half the history of the Three Gorges' development is hidden. The most touching is a Ming-dynasty inscription: a jinshi candidate from Sichuan, on his way to the capital for the imperial examination, passed the Three Wandering Immortals Cave and wrote a poem to express his aspirations. Later, when he successfully passed and returned home, he added beside his original poem the words "and so it came to pass"—this simple yet steadfast "scholar's heart" embodies the unbroken literary lineage that Fan Chengda felt in the cave.

stops.title: Stop Six: Jiujiang—White Deer Grotto Academy, the Holy Land of Neo-Confucianism
stops.content: Passing through Wuhan and entering Jiangxi, Fan Chengda disembarked at Jiangzhou (present-day Jiujiang) to visit the White Deer Grotto Academy at the foot of Lushan Mountain. As the foremost of China's Four Great Academies, the White Deer Grotto Academy had earned worldwide fame through Zhu Xi's lectures here. Fan Chengda and Zhu Xi were contemporaries—though one served as an official in Sichuan and the other taught in Fujian, they held each other in mutual respect. Nestled at the southern foot of Lushan's Five Elders Peak, the academy was surrounded by green mountains, with bubbling springs. Walking through the academy gate, Fan Chengda saw the plaque inscribed with the four characters "White Deer Grotto Academy" and felt a surge of reverence. In his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu, he recorded in detail the academy's layout: the Hall of Confucius, the Imperial Library Pavilion, the Hall of Illuminated Ethics, and more. Though Zhu Xi had already left for Fujian, the students within the academy were still reciting their lessons aloud. Fan Chengda conversed at length with the academy's headmaster, discussing Neo-Confucianism and affairs of state. When he emerged, it was already dusk—mist was rising over Lushan. "How could I know the true face of Lushan, when I am right in the midst of the mountain?"—Su Shi's poem was perfectly apt. The White Deer Grotto Academy reached its pinnacle in the sixth year of the Southern Song Chunxi reign (1179) after its restoration by Zhu Xi—just one year before Fan Chengda passed through, Zhu Xi had left for Fujian. Fan Chengda's description in his Record of a Boat Trip to Wu reveals his deep respect: "The Academy has a Hall of Confucius, where Confucius and his four companions and ten philosophers are worshipped." He noted the ritual regulations of the academy with precision. He also noticed the "Pillow Stream Bridge" before the academy—a natural boulder spanning the stream, "water striking stone and ringing like jade." Students read and debated on the bridge, and the clear sound of their recitation mingled with the gurgling of the stream, forming the most beautiful scene at the White Deer Grotto Academy. Today, the White Deer Grotto Academy remains the most culturally rich site on Lushan. Ancient osmanthus trees tower in its courtyards—the red osmanthus planted by Zhu Xi himself is now over eight hundred years old, still heavy with golden blossoms and fragrant throughout the mountain every autumn. The three characters "White Deer Grotto" before the Hall of Confucius are said to have been inscribed by Li Bo of the Tang—he had lived here in seclusion studying, accompanied by a tame deer, hence the name. From Li Bo to Zhu Xi, from Lu You to Fan Chengda, the White Deer Grotto Academy has been the purest sanctuary for the Chinese scholarly spirit. Here, the gains and losses of official careers, the distances of journeys home, all lose their meaning—only the sound of recitation and the sound of the stream remain, unchanged for a thousand years. Fan Chengda's boat continued eastward, and after passing Jiujiang, it entered the Jiangnan of his dreams—Stone Lake in Suzhou was drawing near.
